summary: Specifies the authentication, authorization, and accounting requirements of cdma2000 wireless data networks, covering roaming among providers for PPP and Mobile IP services.

eli5.summary: It lists what a phone network needs to check who you are and bill you right when you travel.

what is aaa for wireless networks
how does mobile ip work in roaming
subtitle: Security and roaming requirements for CDMA2000 cellular data networks.

tldr.problem: CDMA2000 wireless networks needed to allow users to roam between different carriers and authenticate securely, but there was no standard way to specify how authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) should work in such environments.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a set of requirements for AAA systems in CDMA2000 networks, including how to identify users (by IMSI or NAI), distribute encryption keys, support both PPP and Mobile IP, and enable roaming through broker AAA servers.
tldr.outcome: Equipment vendors and carriers have a clear specification for building interoperable AAA systems, enabling seamless roaming and secure billing across CDMA2000 networks.

today: RFC 3141 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains a foundational document for CDMA2000 carrier networks implementing AAA for roaming services, though the evolution of 3G/4G/5G standards has introduced additional specifications built on these concepts.

sections.title: Roaming and Authentication for Mobile Data
sections.content:
This RFC specifies how CDMA2000 wireless networks should handle authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA) when users roam between carriers. A mobile subscriber visiting a foreign network needs to prove their identity to a home network, which confirms they are a valid customer and will pay the bill.

The document focuses on two service types: traditional PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) and Mobile IP, which allows a mobile device to maintain a constant IP address even when moving between networks. The architecture assumes the subscriber has a relationship with exactly one home carrier, even though they may temporarily connect through visited networks.
sections.eli5: When you drive to another state and use your phone, your phone checks in with a foreign network, which checks with your home network to confirm you are a paying customer. Then you can use data.

sections.title: Network Architecture
sections.content:
The CDMA2000 architecture consists of six main entities. The Radio Network (RN) provides the wireless connection to the mobile device and routes packets. The Packet Data Serving Node (PDSN) acts as a Foreign Agent, establishing links with the mobile, initiating AAA, and tunneling to the Home Agent (HA) if needed.

The AAA Server in the visited network authenticates the mobile and queries the home network's AAA server. The Home Location Register (HLR) and Visitor Location Register (VLR) store authentication data via SS7 signaling. The Mobile Node supports both PPP and Mobile IP, maintaining knowledge of radio resource states.

Broker AAA servers may sit between visited and home networks when the carriers have no direct business relationship, performing protocol translation and rate reconciliation.
sections.eli5: The radio catches the signal, the PDSN acts like a translator, the AAA servers verify you are real, and the Home Agent knows where you live on the Internet.

sections.title: Core AAA Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC requires that AAA systems authenticate a mobile by its NAI (Network Access Identifier) or IMSI (International Mobile Subscriber Identity) in roaming scenarios. The home AAA and serving network AAA must exchange user profile data and AVP (Attribute-Value Pair) attributes securely, encrypting sensitive values across multiple AAA hops.

A reliable transport mechanism is essential: AAA messages must be acknowledged to confirm delivery to the next peer, retransmission must be controlled by the AAA protocol itself (not lower-layer TCP), and the system must detect silent peer failures proactively. Replay protection must prevent attackers from reusing old messages, and accounting messages must be matched with prior authorization to reconcile charges accurately.

Security between AAA servers and between servers and mobile agents (PDSN, HA) must use IP Security (IPsec).
sections.eli5: The networks must verify you are really you, keep their conversation secret, and make sure important messages don't get lost or replayed by hackers.

sections.title: Mobile IP and Key Distribution
sections.content:
Mobile IP in CDMA2000 requires three security associations: between Mobile Node and Foreign Agent (MN-FA), between Foreign Agent and Home Agent (FA-HA), and between Mobile Node and Home Agent (MN-HA). Rather than relying on the IKE key exchange protocol (which may be slow on mobile devices), the RFC allows AAA to distribute keys directly.

The document specifies three features that benefit from AAA-based key distribution. Dynamic Home Agent Assignment lets a visited AAA server assign a Home Agent instead of requiring pre-configuration. Fast Handoff lets the new PDSN use the previous MN-FA extension to authenticate quickly without contacting the home network. HA-FA Authentication provides a pre-shared key so PDSN and HA can authenticate each other without IKE.

Keys and Security Parameter Indexes (SPIs) are encrypted when passed between networks to prevent interception.
sections.eli5: Instead of slow math problems to create secret keys, the AAA system can give out pre-made keys so the handoff is fast and your phone does not run out of battery.

sections.title: Using RFC 2119 Requirements Language
sections.content:
The RFC uses standardized requirement keywords from RFC 2119: MUST means a capability is mandatory, MUST NOT means it is forbidden, SHOULD means it is recommended, and MAY means it is optional. When these words appear in RFC 3141, they describe what AAA protocol submissions MUST be capable of, not what every deployment MUST do.

A protocol submission that satisfies all MUST and MUST NOT requirements is conditionally compliant; one that also satisfies all SHOULD and SHOULD NOT requirements is unconditionally compliant.
sections.eli5: The document uses special words like 'MUST' and 'SHOULD' that have exact meanings so that when engineers read them, they know if something is required or just a good idea.

references.text: Bradner, S., "Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels", BCP 14, RFC 2119, March 1997.
